context: factory · batching plant, casting beds / carousel, curing and gantry-crane yard

brief.intro: New to this project type? A precast factory makes concrete elements — hollow-core slabs, wall panels, beams, columns, stairs — under a roof, then stores them in a yard and ships them to site. Inside the hall there is a concrete batching plant, a way of carrying fresh concrete to the moulds (bucket conveyor or flying bucket), the moulds themselves — long steel beds for prestressed products or a circulating pallet carousel for walls — a reinforcement workshop, and curing. Outside, a large stockyard is served by gantry cranes. The building is simple; the things that drive the programme are the heavy, very flat and accurately levelled foundations for the casting beds and prestressing abutments, the delivery of the production machinery, and the cranes without which nothing can be lifted out of a mould.

glossary.plain: a prestressed floor slab with continuous holes along its length, made on a long bed by a machine.
a long, flat steel bed (often 100 m or more) on which products are cast.
stretching steel strands before the concrete is poured, so the finished element is squeezed and stronger.
the heavy block at each end of a bed that resists the pull of the stressed strands.
the machine that travels along the bed forming the hollow-core slab.
a production line where steel pallets carrying the moulds move from station to station.
a warm, humid store where fresh elements harden quickly.
the concrete strength at which an element may be lifted out of the mould.

must_get_right: Bed and abutment foundations are heavy and must be flat and level to millimetres; they need the machinery supplier's drawings and take longer than the building footings.
Order the production machinery at the start — beds, carousel and batching plant are made to order and set the installation date.
Cranes come before production: the hall cranes and yard gantries must be load-tested before the first element can be lifted.
Allow time for trial mixes, strength results (days of curing) and product certification before the factory can sell.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Vendor drawings → bed, abutment and machine foundations → steel building → roof → floor → cranes → machinery installation → power and utilities → dry runs → trial mixes → first casts → certification. The critical path normally runs through the machinery order and the bed foundations.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late vendor drawings delaying foundations, bed levels out of tolerance, late machinery, crane certification, and slow strength gain delaying product approval. Contingency is held before first cast.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
